title: Orbital Overlap, Sigma and Pi Bonds

pages.title: What holds two hydrogen atoms at one distance?

blocks.text: As two hydrogen atoms approach, attractive interactions can lower the system’s energy. But pushing nuclei very close increases repulsion. A bond forms where the total energy reaches a minimum.
Valence bond theory describes covalent bonding using atomic orbitals and their overlap. The energy minimum explains both a stable distance and the energy needed to separate the atoms.

pages.transition: Balance all the attractions and repulsions during approach.

pages.title: Balance attractions and repulsions

blocks.text: Each hydrogen nucleus attracts both electrons, while nuclei repel one another and electrons repel one another. The total energy depends on all these interactions, not just one attractive force.
At the equilibrium H–H distance, approximately 74 pm, the energy is lower than for separate H atoms. Breaking one mole of gas-phase H–H bonds requires about 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ in the textbook example.

The energy minimum is like the bottom of a valley on a graph of energy against internuclear distance. Moving either closer or farther raises energy relative to that minimum. The valley is a graph analogy, not a literal landscape inside a molecule.

pages.transition: Use orbital overlap to interpret the stabilised arrangement.

pages.title: Overlap singly occupied orbitals

blocks.text: In the elementary valence-bond picture, suitable half-filled atomic orbitals overlap and their electrons pair with opposite spins. Increased electron density between nuclei helps stabilise the bonded arrangement.

Greater effective overlap generally gives a stronger bond for comparable orbitals. Proper orientation matters: two orbitals can occupy nearby space yet overlap inefficiently because their directions or phases do not match.

pages.transition: Distinguish overlap along the bond axis from other orientations.

pages.title: Identify head-on sigma overlap

blocks.text: A sigma bond, σ, forms by head-on overlap along the internuclear axis. Possible examples include s–s, s–p and suitably oriented p–p overlap. Electron density has cylindrical symmetry about the bond axis.
H₂ illustrates 1s–1s σ overlap; HCl can be described using H 1s and an appropriately directed Cl 3p orbital. The σ label describes symmetry, not the element names.

pages.transition: Sideways overlap creates a second symmetry type.

pages.title: Identify sideways pi overlap

blocks.text: A pi bond, π, forms by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals. Electron density lies on opposite sides of the internuclear axis, with a nodal plane containing that axis.

Sideways overlap is generally less effective than comparable head-on overlap, making a π component weaker than its corresponding σ component. The lobes’ phase signs are not positive and negative charges.

pages.transition: Count the components that make single and multiple bonds.

pages.title: Count bonds in single, double and triple links

blocks.text: A conventional single bond is one σ bond. A double bond contains one σ and one π; a triple bond contains one σ and two π bonds. Additional components between the same atoms cannot all be independent head-on σ overlaps.
Thus N≡N has one σ and two π components. A double bond is stronger overall than a comparable single bond, even though its π component is weaker than its σ component.

pages.transition: Orbital alignment explains why rotation can disrupt a π component.

pages.title: Explain restricted rotation around a double bond

blocks.text: Rotating one end of a π bond relative to the other disrupts parallel p-orbital alignment and reduces sideways overlap. This creates a substantial barrier to rotation about a double bond.

A σ bond retains overlap under rotation around its axis much more readily. This orbital argument explains why double bonds constrain molecular arrangement instead of merely adding an extra line on paper.

pages.transition: Methane exposes a limitation of using only pure p directions.

pages.title: Why pure p orbitals cannot explain methane

blocks.text: Carbon’s isolated-atom configuration contains 2s²2p², yet methane has four equivalent C–H bonds directed tetrahedrally. Simply pointing pure p orbitals along perpendicular axes does not reproduce these observations.

Hybridisation mixes atomic orbital functions to construct equivalent directed orbitals. It is a model for describing bonding directions, not four new electrons or an increase in the number of orbitals.

pages.transition: Directed combinations provide the needed tetrahedral description.

pages.title: Introduce the sp³ construction

blocks.text: One s and three p orbitals combine to form four sp³ hybrids. The number of orbitals is conserved. Their directions point tetrahedrally, making angles near 109.5°.

In methane, each carbon hybrid overlaps with H 1s to form a σ bond. The model connects equivalent directional bonding with observed geometry while electron-pair repulsion helps describe deviations when lone pairs occur.

In methane, four carbon hybrids overlap with four separate H 1s orbitals. The four resulting bonds are σ bonds; the sp³ label belongs to the carbon orbital description, not to four new types of hydrogen orbital.

pages.transition: Connect the energy picture with the overlap and geometry vocabulary.

blocks.text: A stable covalent bond corresponds to a lower-energy arrangement at an equilibrium separation. σ and π labels distinguish overlap symmetry; hybridisation supplies useful directed orbital descriptions.
Count components carefully and never confuse orbital phase with charge. Orbital overlap explains why orientation changes bond strength and why π bonds constrain rotation.

questions.question: Why does energy rise if H nuclei approach too closely?
questions.answer: Nucleus–nucleus and other short-range repulsions outweigh further attraction.

questions.question: What does a bond-energy minimum identify?
questions.answer: A stable equilibrium internuclear separation relative to nearby distances.

questions.question: How does a σ bond differ from a π bond?
questions.answer: σ uses head-on overlap along the axis; π uses sideways parallel overlap with density off the axis.

questions.question: Count components of a conventional triple bond.
questions.answer: One σ and two π bonds.

questions.question: Why does double-bond rotation require substantial energy?
questions.answer: Rotation disrupts the parallel orbital alignment needed for π overlap.

questions.question: How many hybrids arise from one s and three p orbitals?
questions.answer: Four sp³ orbitals; mixing conserves the number of orbitals.

questions.question: Why is methane not explained by three pure perpendicular p bonds?
questions.answer: It has four equivalent bonds with tetrahedral rather than 90° directions.
